title: Job 20:12–29
context: Zophar continues, with images of wickedness as food that is sweet at first but turns to poison, riches swallowed and then given back, and an oppressor of the poor who cannot keep what he has seized. He describes God’s wrath raining on the wicked, weapons and terrors overtaking him, fire consuming his tent, and heaven and earth rising up against him, and closes, “This is the portion of a wicked man from God.” Both traditions affirm that sin carries real consequences and that God opposes oppression, while reading the speech as Zophar’s view, which the book does not endorse as an account of Job’s suffering (42:7).

verses.text: “Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue.” Arminian readers note the image of sin enjoyed and savored.

Scripture often describes sin as pleasant at first and bitter later (cf. Prov 20:17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the deceptive sweetness of sin.

Shared ground: both traditions agree with the general truth of the image, while noting that Zophar uses it to suggest that Job is hiding secret sin.

verses.text: though he spare it, and will not let it go, but keep it still within his mouth,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar continues, “though he spare it, and will not let it go, but keep it still within his mouth.” Arminian readers note the picture of clinging to sin and refusing to give it up.

The image depicts a will attached to wrongdoing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the grip that sin can have on the heart.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a true observation about sin, while recognizing that the book does not support Zophar’s application of it to Job.

verses.text: yet his food in his bowels is turned. It is cobra venom within him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says, “yet his food in his bowels is turned. It is cobra venom within him.” Arminian readers note the reversal from sweetness to poison.

Sin’s pleasures turn into harm.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the self-destructive nature of sin.

Shared ground: both traditions agree with the moral point, and both remember that the book later rejects the friends’ assumption that Job’s suffering is such a punishment.

verses.text: He has swallowed down riches, and he will vomit them up again. God will cast them out of his belly.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He has swallowed down riches, and he will vomit them up again. God will cast them out of his belly.” Arminian readers note that Zophar names God as the one who reverses ill-gotten gain.

The image is blunt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see divine justice depicted in strong language.

Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God does not let injustice stand forever, while reading this as Zophar’s picture rather than the book’s account of how God dealt with Job.

verses.text: He will suck cobra venom. The viper’s tongue will kill him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will suck cobra venom. The viper’s tongue will kill him.” Arminian readers note that the poison image continues.

The wicked man is destroyed by what he took in.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see sin’s consequences returning on the sinner.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that sin brings its own harm (cf. Gal 6:7–8), while keeping Zophar’s speech distinct from the book’s verdict.

verses.text: He will not look at the rivers, the flowing streams of honey and butter.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will not look at the rivers, the flowing streams of honey and butter.” Arminian readers note the image of abundance denied.

The wicked man loses the blessings he hoped to enjoy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the loss of enjoyment that Zophar predicts for the wicked.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that true satisfaction is not found in plunder, and both read the verse as part of Zophar’s poem rather than a description of Job.

verses.text: He will restore that for which he labored, and will not swallow it down. He will not rejoice according to the substance that he has gotten.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will restore that for which he labored, and will not swallow it down.” Arminian readers note the theme of restitution.

The gain does not remain with the one who seized it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the futility of gain without righteousness.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that ill-gotten gain does not last, and both note that the book’s own ending, where Job is restored, does not follow Zophar’s logic.

verses.text: For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor. He has violently taken away a house, and he will not build it up.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor. He has violently taken away a house.” Arminian readers note that Zophar names oppression of the poor as the wicked man’s sin.

Eliphaz will later accuse Job of such sins directly (22:6–9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s concern for the poor reflected here.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that oppressing the poor is grave sin, while noting that the book presents Job as innocent of such charges (cf. 29:12–17; 31:16–22).

verses.text: “Because he knew no quietness within him, he will not save anything of that in which he delights.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Because he knew no quietness within him, he will not save anything of that in which he delights.” Arminian readers note the inner restlessness Zophar attributes to the wicked.

Greed leaves no peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the emptiness of a heart never satisfied.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that contentment is found in God, not in possessions (cf. Phil 4:11–13), while reading the verse as Zophar’s description.

verses.text: There was nothing left that he didn’t devour, therefore his prosperity will not endure.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There was nothing left that he didn’t devour, therefore his prosperity will not endure.” Arminian readers note the link Zophar draws between greed and loss.

The principle has general wisdom behind it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see greed undermining its own success.

Shared ground: both traditions affirm the general truth while noting that Zophar treats it as a law without exceptions, which Job will dispute.

verses.text: In the fullness of his sufficiency, distress will overtake him. The hand of everyone who is in misery will come on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the fullness of his sufficiency, distress will overtake him.” Arminian readers note that Zophar claims trouble comes at the height of prosperity.

The picture is of sudden reversal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the insecurity of wealth gained unjustly.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that riches cannot guarantee safety (cf. Prov 23:5), and both read the verse as part of Zophar’s argument.

verses.text: When he is about to fill his belly, God will cast the fierceness of his wrath on him. It will rain on him while he is eating.
verses.arminianNotes:
“God will cast the fierceness of his wrath on him. It will rain on him while he is eating.” Arminian readers note that Zophar describes God’s wrath as falling suddenly.

He is confident about how and when God judges.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see divine judgment pictured in vivid terms.

Shared ground: both traditions affirm God’s wrath against sin, while recognizing that the friends claim to know the timing and form of judgment more confidently than the book allows.

verses.text: He will flee from the iron weapon. The bronze arrow will strike him through.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will flee from the iron weapon. The bronze arrow will strike him through.” Arminian readers note the image of inescapable judgment.

Escape from one danger leads into another.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of judgment in Zophar’s picture.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse briefly as Zophar’s poetry about the end of the wicked, without applying it to Job.

verses.text: He draws it out, and it comes out of his body. Yes, the glittering point comes out of his liver. Terrors are on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar continues the image of the arrow and says, “Terrors are on him.” Arminian readers note the emphasis on fear.

The picture is of a man undone by dread.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the terror that accompanies judgment in Zophar’s description (cf. 18:11).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly and briefly as part of the friends’ repeated portrait of the wicked.

verses.text: All darkness is laid up for his treasures. An unfanned fire will devour him. It will consume that which is left in his tent.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All darkness is laid up for his treasures. An unfanned fire will devour him.” Arminian readers note the images of darkness and fire.

The “unfanned fire” suggests a judgment not kindled by human hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see divine judgment implied.

Shared ground: both traditions read the images as Zophar’s description, and both remember that fire had fallen on Job’s flocks (1:16), which may make Zophar’s words more pointed.

verses.text: The heavens will reveal his iniquity. The earth will rise up against him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The heavens will reveal his iniquity. The earth will rise up against him.” Arminian readers note that Zophar calls heaven and earth as witnesses against the wicked.

Some read this as a reply to Job’s hope of a witness in heaven (16:18–19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the possible reversal of Job’s words, hedged as a reading.

Shared ground: both traditions see the debate sharpening as Zophar turns the language of witness against Job’s hope.

verses.text: The increase of his house will depart. They will rush away in the day of his wrath.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The increase of his house will depart. They will rush away in the day of his wrath.” Arminian readers note the loss of household wealth.

The “day of his wrath” refers to God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the end of the wicked man’s prosperity.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Zophar’s view, and both note that Job had already lost his household goods (1:13–19), which gives the words a painful edge.

verses.text: This is the portion of a wicked man from God, the heritage appointed to him by God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“This is the portion of a wicked man from God, the heritage appointed to him by God.” Arminian readers note that Zophar closes with a confident summary.

Job uses similar words in 27:13; how the two passages relate is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a firm statement of retribution.

Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God judges the wicked, while remembering that Zophar’s application is his own and is not the book’s last word.
